Behind Block C of Sunrise Colony, where the parking light kept flickering, three older boys were passing a vape around. One of them held it out to Sangeeta.
"Just one. Don't be a baby."
"No thanks," she said. "I get dizzy on the swing, imagine this."
A couple of them snorted. "Seriously, try it."
"Seriously, no." She kept her voice light and glanced at Farhan, who was already standing up and dusting off his jeans.
"My mum's making pakoras," Farhan said. "Sangeeta, you coming?"
"Coming."
They walked off toward the lit staircase. Someone behind them muttered "boring", and then the talk moved on to cricket. On the second floor landing Sangeeta let out a long breath.
"Thanks for getting up first."
Farhan shrugged. "You'd have done it for me."

qa.q: What reason did Farhan give for leaving?
qa.a: Farhan said his mum was making pakoras.

qa.q: How can you tell Sangeeta felt more tense than she showed?
qa.a: She let out a long breath on the landing and thanked Farhan for getting up first, so her light voice was covering real nerves.

qa.q: Which parts of Sangeeta's refusal worked, and why?
qa.a: A short "no thanks", a joke about getting dizzy, and then leaving with Farhan gave the older boys nothing to argue with, so the pressure faded quickly.

qa.q: What would change if Farhan had stayed sitting down?
qa.a: Sangeeta would have been the only one saying no, which is much harder, and the older boys might have kept pushing her.

grounding: A teenage girl turns down a vape with a calm no and a joke and walks away, made easier because Farhan stands up and leaves with her.

passage:
"Seema, we're going up to the terrace after lights out. Sir sleeps by ten."
"Isn't the terrace door locked?"
"Lock's broken. You in?"
"I'm out. I've got a full night of snoring planned."
"Come on, Seema, everyone's going."
"Then the terrace will be full without me. Good night, Jatin."
"You'll regret it tomorrow."
"Maybe. Raghav, you're staying down here?"
"Obviously. I'm scared of heights and of Sir."
Jatin rolled his eyes and walked off down the guesthouse corridor. Seema sat down on the bench by the water cooler.
"Honestly, my heart was going so fast," she said.
"Didn't look like it."
"It's easier when one more person says no."
"Next time you say it first and I'll back you. Deal?"
"Deal. Now give me one of those biscuits."

qa.q: What joke does Seema make when she says no?
qa.a: Seema says she has a full night of snoring planned.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling while she refused, and how do we know?
qa.a: Seema was nervous; she admits her heart was going so fast even though she sounded calm.

qa.q: What made Seema's refusal work without a fight?
qa.a: She gave a short no, added a joke, wished Jatin good night instead of arguing, and Raghav stayed with her, so she was not standing alone.

qa.q: How might Jatin see Seema's answer?
qa.a: Jatin may feel annoyed that his plan looks less exciting, but because Seema stayed friendly he had nothing to fight with except "You'll regret it".

grounding: On a trip a teenager says no to sneaking onto a terrace with a joke and a calm good night, and Raghav staying behind too makes it easier.

passage:
I'm Manoj, and last Diwali I learnt something about saying no.
Behind the community hall, some older guys were passing around a bottle. One of them held it out to me. "Just a sip, Manoj. Don't be a kid."
My heart was thumping, but I kept it short. "Nah, I'm good. My mum can smell things from three streets away." A couple of them laughed. Then I said I had to help with the rangoli and walked back toward the lights.
What made it easy was Divyansh. Before we went back there, we had agreed: if either of us says "rangoli", we both leave. He came with me without a word.
Nobody chased us. The next day one of the older guys even nodded at me at the shop. Having one person on my side made that no feel half as heavy.

qa.q: What code word had Manoj and Divyansh agreed on?
qa.a: They agreed that if either of them says 'rangoli', they both leave.

qa.q: How was Manoj feeling when the bottle was held out, and what shows it?
qa.a: Manoj was nervous, with a thumping heart, yet kept the refusal short and light with a joke about Mum.

qa.q: Which parts of Manoj's refusal kept it from turning into a fight?
qa.a: A short no, a joke that got a laugh, a simple reason to leave, and a friend who left too, so there was nothing to argue with.

qa.q: What was it like for Divyansh to have the plan agreed beforehand?
qa.a: Divyansh did not have to decide or argue in the moment; he could just walk away beside Manoj, so neither of them stood alone.

grounding: Shows a teenager refusing with a calm no and a joke, then leaving with a friend, and how that ally made the refusal lighter.

passage:
Coach's note, inter-school tournament, night two
Around 10 pm I heard voices in the hostel corridor. Four of the under-16 players were planning to slip out to the night market. I waited behind the door for a moment instead of storming in.
Kavin said, "Mridul, you're coming. Don't spoil it."
Mridul answered, calm and short: "No, bro. My legs are dead, and I want to start tomorrow." Then he laughed. "Also, Coach sleeps like a cat." He picked up his water bottle and went back toward his room.
Farida, standing beside him, said at once, "Same. Goodnight, legends," and followed.
Nobody argued after that. The plan fizzled in two minutes.
What I did next: at breakfast I went over the tournament rules with the whole squad and why they exist. Privately I thanked Mridul and Farida, and I've put both names down for the team-captain workshop.

qa.q: Where were the four players planning to go?
qa.a: They were planning to slip out to the night market.

qa.q: What does Mridul's short answer and laugh suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Mridul seemed calm and sure of the choice; the joke about Coach kept it light, so it did not sound like a lecture.

qa.q: How did the coach follow up the next morning?
qa.a: The coach went over the tournament rules with the whole squad at breakfast and privately thanked Mridul and Farida.

qa.q: How might Kavin have felt when Farida backed Mridul up?
qa.a: Kavin probably felt the plan lose its pull; with two people saying a calm no together, there was no one left to argue with.

grounding: Shows a teenager turning down a night-time sneak-out with a short no and a joke, with a teammate backing the refusal, as noted by the coach.

passage:
Tuesday night
Today at lunch Omkar had photos of tomorrow's chemistry answers on his phone. Everyone crowded round. He shoved it at me: "Take it, Jatin, everyone's copying."
I said, "Nah, man. I'd copy it wrong anyway, you've seen my handwriting." They laughed, and I said I had to return a book and walked off to the library. My ears were burning the whole way.
Ten minutes later Pradeep dropped into the chair next to me. "Too crowded there," he said. That's all. We did two past papers together till the bell.
I don't even know if the photos were real. After school I told Sen ma'am quietly that answers might be going round, without naming anyone. She said thanks and that she'd handle it.
I'm glad I didn't have to argue, and gladder Pradeep came. If he hadn't, I might have gone back.
Jatin

qa.q: What did Omkar have on his phone at lunch?
qa.a: Omkar had photos of tomorrow's chemistry answers.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel walking to the library, and what shows it?
qa.a: Jatin felt embarrassed and tense; Jatin's ears were burning the whole way even though the refusal had worked.

qa.q: What made Jatin's refusal work without an argument?
qa.a: A joke about bad handwriting, a simple excuse about returning a book and leaving straight away, followed by a quiet word to Sen ma'am.

qa.q: How might Pradeep have seen Jatin's walk-out?
qa.a: Pradeep may have been uneasy about copying too, and Jatin leaving first gave Pradeep an easy way to follow without making a speech.

grounding: Shows a teenager refusing leaked answers with a joke and an excuse, leaving, and being joined by a friend whose support made it easier.
